course.title: From expansions to square differences and odd gaps
course.sourceAnchor: AoPS Introduction to Algebra2007 section11.2, printed313-314; catalogue row681; follows publication802/1
course.editionAnchor: AoPS First Printing2007; original authored unit803/1
course.rightsAnchor: Original paraphrased instructional activities with source/page metadata. Textbook bytes are excluded; third-party rights and repository license remain separate and unresolved.

nodes.title: Recall every product
nodes.body: Reconstruct a product table for (x+1)*(x+1). Identify which products contribute to each degree. This recalls publication802/1 before using expansion to explain a new pattern.
nodes.hint: List the four products before collecting powers.
nodes.exercise: Explain the role of each cross product.

nodes.title: Worked bridge to a difference
nodes.body: Expand (n+1)*(n+1), then subtract n*n. Equal-term subtraction leaves2*n+1, an odd number. This argument never divides by a term that might be zero.
nodes.worked: For n=6, the two squares49 and36 differ by13=2*6+1. This example illustrates the identity; expansion justifies arbitrary natural n.
nodes.hint: Separate the common square from its remainder.
nodes.exercise: Explain why the common square disappears.

nodes.title: State the domain and claim
nodes.body: State the universal consecutive-square gap claim for n in Nat. Explain why matching the pattern at n=2,3,4 supports a conjecture but does not prove it for every n.
nodes.exercise: State the quantifier and what must be justified.
nodes.hint: Compare a finite list with an arbitrary natural input.

nodes.title: Check the exact precursor
nodes.body: Use the fixed exact goal (x+1)*(x+1) over Q[x]. Enter constant, linear and quadratic coefficients. This checks the precursor expansion; it does not check the later written proof or a conjugate factorization.
nodes.hint: Compare each coefficient with your product table.

nodes.title: Find the invalid cancellation
nodes.body: A proposed proof assumes equal positive integers a=b, factors a difference, then divides by a-b to claim a contradiction. Identify the first illegal operation. Explain why positivity of a cannot justify that division.
nodes.exercise: Give the missing nonzero assumption and an equal-input example.
nodes.hint: Evaluate the divisor using the stated equality before cancelling.

nodes.title: Independent proof of every odd gap
nodes.body: Without hints, prove that the gap between consecutive squares is2*n+1 for every n in Nat. Justify expansion and subtraction. A Lean reference checks the algebraic equality; your written argument still needs human review.

nodes.title: Transfer to integer-pair classification
nodes.body: Find all positive integer pairs u>v whose square difference is45. Use (u-v)*(u+v), explain its parity constraint and show your list is exhaustive. This new problem is human-reviewed.
nodes.exercise: Classify all positive u>v with u*u-v*v=45 and justify completeness.
nodes.hint: Write the factor pairs of45 and recover u and v from each sum and difference.

nodes.title: Later independent reconstruction
nodes.body: After the scheduled delay, reconstruct the consecutive-square proof without hints. Explain when a difference factors into conjugates and why dividing by a zero difference invalidates an argument.
nodes.review: Seven-day authored review; completion requires a linked response and exact or versioned human assessment. The schedule alone is not evidence of retention.
nodes.exercise: Reconstruct a universal proof and diagnose a fresh invalid cancellation.

learningGoals: Use the expansion in802/1 to justify every consecutive-square gap
Account for cancelling cross terms in conjugate products
Distinguish identities from division by a possibly zero term
Classify possible integer pairs by parity of conjugate factors
notationGuide: Prerequisite publication802/1: all four products and both cross terms
The informal conjugate identity is over Z; the reference successor theorem is over Nat
The exact checker supports only the marked fixed polynomial precursor; other work requires human review
A pattern at finitely many inputs does not prove a universal identity
